newsitem.title: USA: Relics of US-Soviet space race at Air-Space museum.
newsitem.headline: Relics of US-Soviet space race at Air-Space museum.

text.p: Relics of the Cold War space race, including an "Ivan Ivanovich" space dummy and a never-used Soviet moon suit, went on display on Thursday, thanks in part to billionaire Ross Perot.

Perot bought some of the artifacts at Sotheby's auction house in 1993 for about $4 million, but kept his role in the matter private until now, organisers of the exhibit at the National Air and Space Museum in Washington said.

The museum needed Perot's help, organisers said, because they could not afford to purchase the items on their own. About $3 million worth of Perot's pieces are included in the show. Other items were loaned by the Russian space museum at Star City.

Speaking in front of massive pieces of the exhibit, including a bus-sized craft composed of the silver-and-white U.S. Apollo module linked with a rounded light-green Soviet era Soyuz TM-10, Perot said he wanted the artifacts to be kept together and possibly returned to Russia someday.

"When I first got the Sotheby's catalogue ... my reaction was that these are invaluable historical artifacts," Perot said at a press preview of the show. "... My concern was that these artifacts would be distributed and could never be pulled back together. I felt strongly that this is part of Russia's heritage."

The exhibit includes a Russian moon suit, developed but never used, that features a backpack that swings open like a cupboard door to let the cosmonaut get inside. That was displayed in a case next to a U.S. moon suit used in 1971, still covered with moon dust.

An "Ivan Ivanovich" mannequin sent into space was exhibited nearby, along with astronaut John Glenn's silver, zipper-riddled spacesuit and a baggy orange training suit used by Yuri Gagarin, the first person in space.
This was not the first time the museum showed Soviet-vintage materials. Also on display is the last remaining piece of the first human-made satellite, the Sputnik.

Hours after the space shuttle Atlantis blasted off on Thursday for a rendezvous with the Russian space station Mir to pick up U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger, and amid controversey over U.S.-Russian cooperation on an international space station, two former space travelers recalled their own personal experiences with pieces in the space exhibit.

Aleksei Leonov, the first person to walk in space, recalled using the same kind of space-walking suit displayed at the museum, but had to be prompted by Perot to tell the tale of how he got stranded outside his spacecraft.
"This is the man who took the first walk in space," Perot told reporters. "This is the man who, when he got out there, couldn't get back in. Get him to tell that story."

"After my walk in space, when I come back to spacecraft, I have a little emergency situation. My spacesuit had a deformation ... I believe condition of my spacesuit was OK because I am speaking now with you," Leonov said.
In Perot's version, Leonov risked letting air out of his spacesuit -- "which could have caused his body to explode" -- so he could return to the spacecraft.
Former U.S. astronaut Thomas Stafford, who was part of the Apollo-Soyuz team, said he expected continued cooperation in space with Russia.
"The long-range goal is ... to continue on this exploration and someday I feel we're going to go to Mars together," Stafford said.
The exhibit opens to the public on Friday.
